explanations.explanation: It's her beloved at the door, friend. She says, "A sound! My beloved is knocking…" (Song of Solomon 5:2). Then he speaks up himself: "Open to me, my sister, my darling, my dove, my flawless one." Knocking in the middle of the night means he really wants in.

The watchmen are in this song, but not yet. They show up in verse 7, walking their rounds of the city. The knock in verse 2 belongs to her beloved, and he's the one saying, "Open to me." So hold onto the watchmen, because they come later.

The daughters of Jerusalem are a group of women in this song, and they don't show up until later. She talks to them in verse 8 and they answer in verse 9. The one at her door in the night is her beloved. He's even got dew on his head from being out there.

Open is it. He says, "Open to me…" and then tells her his head is drenched with dew and his hair with the dampness of the night. Nobody says that from a warm porch. I think a man dripping like that wants a door that swings.
Close, since she does hear him. But he doesn't ask her to listen. What he says is "Open to me…" (Song of Solomon 5:2). She already heard the knock, so what he's asking for is the door.

This whole book is a song, so I see why you went there. But he never asks her to sing a note. He says, "Open to me, my sister, my darling, my dove, my flawless one." The request is about the door, and the dew on his head tells you he's out in the night.

explanations.answer: If she must put her robe back on
explanations.explanation: That's what she says: "I have taken off my robe—must I put it back on?" She adds that she's washed her feet and asks, "must I soil them again?" (Song of Solomon 5:3). A knock came right when she'd settled in. I'd be standing there in the dark wondering the same thing.

explanations.answer: Why he came so late tonight
explanations.explanation: That's a fair thing to wonder, but she doesn't say it. Her questions in this verse are about her robe and her feet. She asks if she must put the robe back on and if she must soil her washed feet again.

explanations.answer: Whether the door is even locked
explanations.explanation: The text doesn't have her checking any locks here. Her questions are about getting dressed again: "must I put it back on?" and "must I soil them again?" (Song of Solomon 5:3). A bolt does show up in verse 5, but only when she goes to open it.

Her heart, friend. "My beloved put his hand to the latch; my heart pounded for him" (Song of Solomon 5:4). Back in verse 2 she said her heart was awake while she slept. That heart does not sit still when he's close.

No fists here. Nobody's fighting anybody, and the one pounding in this verse is her heart. "My beloved put his hand to the latch; my heart pounded for him." It's a love song, so the pounding is on the inside.

I get why feet came to mind, since she did just wash hers in verse 3. But in verse 4 the pounding is her heart. "My beloved put his hand to the latch; my heart pounded for him." Her clean feet are just standing there, hoping not to get dirty.
The text says the opposite. She says, "I rose up to open for my beloved" (Song of Solomon 5:5). Her robe question doesn't keep her in bed. She gets up and goes to the door.

False is right. She says, "I rose up to open for my beloved," and then, "I opened for my beloved" (Song of Solomon 5:5-6). She wondered about the robe, but then she got up. A little grumbling about comfort didn't stop her.

That's what she finds: "I opened for my beloved, but he had turned and gone." Then comes, "My heart sank at his departure" (Song of Solomon 5:6). She did get up and open the door, and he wasn't there. I think that's a hard moment, and I'd say it's okay to feel it.

explanations.answer: He is still at the door
explanations.explanation: If only. The text says, "I opened for my beloved, but he had turned and gone" (Song of Solomon 5:6). The doorway is empty, and her heart sinks at his departure.

explanations.answer: He is waiting down the street
explanations.explanation: The text never puts him down the street. It says he "had turned and gone," and she "sought him but did not find him" (Song of Solomon 5:6). He's out of sight, and she doesn't know where he went.

True. She says, "I sought him but did not find him. I called, but he did not answer" (Song of Solomon 5:6). She's looking and she's calling, and all she gets back is quiet. I think that quiet is the heaviest part of this verse.

The text says the opposite. She says, "I sought him but did not find him. I called, but he did not answer" (Song of Solomon 5:6). She calls out and no answer comes back. It's a heavy moment, so no joke from me here.

explanations.answer: That she is sick with love
explanations.explanation: That's her message: "if you find my beloved, tell him I am sick with love" (Song of Solomon 5:8). She's just been beaten and lost her cloak, but that's not what she sends. She sends what's in her heart. It's a short message, and I think it says everything.
The watchmen did beat and bruise her in verse 7. But that's not what she asks the daughters to say. Her message is, "tell him I am sick with love" (Song of Solomon 5:8).

explanations.answer: That she is tired of waiting
explanations.explanation: She never says that in the text. What she tells the daughters of Jerusalem to say is, "tell him I am sick with love" (Song of Solomon 5:8). Her whole message is about her love for him.

Beautiful it is. They ask, "How is your beloved better than others, O most beautiful among women?" (Song of Solomon 5:9). They say it twice, in verses 9 and 6:1. Those women have some real respect for her.
Faithful is a nice word, but it's not theirs. They call her "most beautiful among women" (Song of Solomon 5:9). They say it again in 6:1 when they ask where her beloved has gone.

Patient didn't make it into their question. The daughters of Jerusalem say, "O most beautiful among women" (Song of Solomon 5:9). They say it again in 6:1. Whatever she's feeling in this scene, they see her as the most beautiful.

explanations.answer: She paints a picture of what he's like
explanations.explanation: She sure does. From verse 10 through 16 she describes him from his head down: gold, a raven's black hair, eyes like doves, lips like lilies. She doesn't give a short answer. She gives them the whole portrait.

explanations.answer: She says they'll know him when they see him
explanations.explanation: She's got way more to say than that. Instead of leaving it to guesswork, she starts right in with "My beloved is dazzling and ruddy, outstanding among ten thousand" (Song of Solomon 5:10). Then she keeps going for six more verses.

explanations.answer: She tells them to go ask the watchmen
explanations.explanation: The watchmen are the ones who beat her in verse 7, so I think she's not sending anyone to them. She answers the question herself. "My beloved is dazzling and ruddy, outstanding among ten thousand" (Song of Solomon 5:10), and that's only the start of her answer.

explanations.answer: No one else compares to him
explanations.explanation: That's the heart of it. Ten thousand is a big crowd, and she says he is "outstanding among ten thousand" (Song of Solomon 5:10). She picks him out of all of them. In her eyes, nobody stands next to him.

explanations.answer: He leads an army of thousands
explanations.explanation: The text doesn't say anything about an army. The words are "outstanding among ten thousand" (Song of Solomon 5:10). It's a way of saying he stands above the crowd. The only flock in this passage is the one in 6:2.

explanations.answer: He is hard to pick out in a crowd
explanations.explanation: It's actually the reverse. "Outstanding" means he stands out. She says he's outstanding among ten thousand, so out of that whole crowd, he's the one you'd notice.
She goes in the other direction. She opens with "His head is purest gold" (Song of Solomon 5:11). The legs don't come until verse 15, near the end. So she works from the top down.

False is right. She starts at the top with "His head is purest gold" (Song of Solomon 5:11). Then come his eyes, cheeks, lips, arms and body, and his legs near the end in verse 15. Head first, feet last.

explanations.answer: He is her companion as well as her love
explanations.explanation: That's it. She says, "This is my beloved, and this is my friend" (Song of Solomon 5:16). He isn't one or the other. He's both her love and her friend, and I think that's a good thing to have in one person.

explanations.answer: He is only a friend to her from now on
explanations.explanation: She doesn't swap one word for the other. She says, "This is my beloved, and this is my friend" (Song of Solomon 5:16). She uses both words together. She doesn't take anything away.

explanations.answer: He is a friend to the daughters as well
explanations.explanation: Look at the word she uses: "my friend." She says, "This is my beloved, and this is my friend, O daughters of Jerusalem" (Song of Solomon 5:16). She's talking to them, but she's telling them what he is to her.
Seek, friend. The daughters of Jerusalem say, "We will seek him with you" (Song of Solomon 6:1). Earlier she had gone out and "sought him but did not find him." Now she's got company on the search.
Greeting him sounds polite, but that's not their offer. They say, "We will seek him with you" (Song of Solomon 6:1). They'll go looking right alongside her.
Nobody's warning anyone. The daughters of Jerusalem say, "We will seek him with you" (Song of Solomon 6:1). They offer to join her search.

explanations.answer: She tells them where he has gone
explanations.explanation: She does. "My beloved has gone down to his garden, to the beds of spices, to pasture his flock in the gardens and to gather lilies" (Song of Solomon 6:2). Back in 5:6 she couldn't find him. Now she has an answer ready.

explanations.answer: She says she will search alone
explanations.explanation: She doesn't say that. The daughters offered, "We will seek him with you," and her reply is about where he is: "My beloved has gone down to his garden…" (Song of Solomon 6:2). She never turns them down.

explanations.answer: She asks them to wait until morning
explanations.explanation: No waiting is mentioned anywhere. She answers right away: "My beloved has gone down to his garden, to the beds of spices…" (Song of Solomon 6:2). She tells them where he is.

True. She says, "I belong to my beloved and he belongs to me" (Song of Solomon 6:3). That comes right after the empty doorway and the long search. I think it's a strong thing to say after a night like that.
The text says otherwise. She says, "I belong to my beloved and he belongs to me" (Song of Solomon 6:3). It comes right after the empty doorway. She says they belong to each other.
